body.text: With just four weeks to go until the US midterm elections a “blue wave” — or what Australians would call a Democratic landslide — seems likely. The Democrats are eight points ahead in national polls and have a lead in key Senate races like Texas and Ohio. Some real long-shots have moved from highly implausible to conceivable. A couple of polls show them ahead in Kansas, a state that has not returned a Democratic senator since 1932. Election analysts like Nate Silver and G. Elliott Morris think the chances of a major Democratic win are being underestimated in Washington.

It is not hard to understand why the Republicans’ position is deteriorating. Trump’s personal ratings have continued to fall. His disastrous war in Iran has pushed up prices, and his antics are getting ever more absurd and distant from the interests of Americans. No political consultant would recommend choosing now to focus on renaming AI as “superintelligence” or a grotesque new ballroom in the White House. As this Economist chart shows, he is well below his first-term lows, or Biden’s lowest point. (Trump’s current trajectory is the heavy red line.)

Yet there has been surprisingly little commentary about what it would mean for American, and global, politics if the Democrats do take both chambers on 3 November. This is partly because Republicans dare not suggest Trump might be fallible, and liberals don’t want to tempt fate. This is an understandable instinct. We have seen fairly substantial polling errors in the past, and there is a residual fear that a desperate Trump will do anything to try to stop a Democratic victory. But there is not a lot he can do in practice, beyond attempting a coup. The states run elections, not the federal government.

If they’re as successful as they look like being, what could the Democrats do with congressional power? What would that mean for the war in Iran? What happens if we get a full-blown war between the executive and legislative branches? And what would it all mean for politics in other countries?

If the Democrats take control of the House — regardless of what happens in the Senate — we will see a raft of investigations launched into Trump’s behaviour over the past two years. When they won the House in 2018 the Democrats ran more than a dozen investigations, including into Trump’s relationship with Russia, dodgy financial transactions, and pressure on the Ukrainians to investigate the Bidens — which triggered Trump’s first impeachment.

This time around they would have an even more egregious set of misdemeanours to investigate. The Epstein files would probably be top of the list, due to the level of public interest and because the issue can be used to increase tensions among Republicans. Then there are dozens of other potential avenues around Trump’s personal corruption, which has been barely disguised in his second term: his cryptocurrency initiatives, his Qatari jet, son-in-law Jared Kushner’s business dealings in the Middle East, alleged manipulation of prediction markets and so on. There is the war in Iran, and whether he ignored warnings about what would happen, as well as Pete Hegseth’s role and his terrible relationship with the military. And all this is before we get to domestic administrative issues like the DOGE fiasco, ICE agents breaking the law, and political intimidation by the Justice Department. The Democrats won’t be short of material.

But 2018–20 also showed the limitations of these powers when they’re confronted by a president who has no interest in institutional norms or the appearance of propriety. Widespread non-cooperation with investigations included refusals to comply with subpoenas in the knowledge that forcing compliance via the courts would take too long. The White House knew it could run down the clock. It could also block any criminal contempt charges voted through in the House because those have to be prosecuted by the Justice Department, which Trump had filled with yes-men.

Investigations can still make life a pain for the administration. Committees can subpoena third parties and former members of Trump’s team, who are less likely to ignore the personal legal risk. And they can publish documents provided by whistleblowers. But it is a frustrating process. In a normal world, the House would have other levers to try to force compliance, such as blocking Republican legislation. But most of the time that is not a huge issue for Trump as he doesn’t have much he wants to pass and prefers to rule by executive fiat.

One difference this time, though, is that the Democrats might control all of Congress. The Senate has additional leverage because it signs off on appointments to senior executive roles and the judiciary. Again, this is less of a bargaining chip than it would be with other presidents, because Trump has no interest in good administration or the institutional balance of power once he has gone. But it may prove valuable if Trump is determined to push particular individuals through the confirmation process. It may also encourage some Republican representatives and senators to start compromising, regardless of what the president says.
Ultimately, exactly how aggressive the battle between Congress and the executive gets will depend on politics more than process.

The prime factor is the extent of the Democratic victory, assuming there is one. If they win the Senate 51–49, then it only takes one member of the caucus to defect for them to lose a majority. Congressional voting is much more polarised than it used to be but there are still a few Democrats who will sometimes defect because they want to seem willing to compromise or have shifted ideologically rightwards.

The most obvious example is Pennsylvania senator John Fetterman, who has been the sole Democrat voting with the Republicans on forty-five occasions, including supporting the confirmation of Pam Bondi as attorney-general and opposing measures restricting military action against Iran. But the New Hampshire senators, Jeanne Shaheen and Maggie Hassan, as well as the nominally independent Angus King of Maine, also sometimes defect. The bigger the majority the greater the opportunity for the Democrats to pursue a more combative strategy.

With a more secure majority, internal Democratic politics would drive a “blue” Congress towards tougher action. The next two years will be dominated by jockeying in both parties to be the presidential nominee. Most Democratic voters are extremely angry and looking for decisive action against Trump. Establishment senators and donors are desperate to avoid a serious challenge from the left of the party, with Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez the most plausible candidate. All potential candidates will want to show their willingness to play rough, pushing Congress towards confrontation.
The dynamics of anything other than a very narrow win point towards rapid escalation.

The US Constitution is not designed for this scenario. The Founders assumed there would be conflict from time to time, and so built in checks and balances. But they did not imagine the level of polarisation in party politics could reach the point where one party would simply refuse to remove a president regardless of how badly he behaved. Nor did they envisage the vast state apparatus Trump now controls, or the gradual shift to greater executive power as successive presidents have found ways to work around Congress’s nominal powers, like the ability to declare war and control government spending. Courts have been reluctant to resolve disputes in favour of Congress, and presidents’ ability to move faster than the legislature has given them a much stronger position than was initially intended.
So what could a determined Congress do?

Impeachment remains its strongest tool. But to actually remove the president, or one of his team, requires a two-thirds majority in the Senate. Trump will surely be impeached for the third time at some point in the next two years. It is not completely inconceivable that it could work this time, given he will be an extremely unpopular lame-duck president and more Republicans will be looking for ways to escape his shadow. But it remains extremely unlikely, because Trump can still use his influence to defeat party opponents in primaries. Anyone who wants a shot at the Republican presidential nomination for 2028 will have to keep paying fealty and attack any colleague who defects.

It is marginally more plausible that Hegseth will be removed. He will almost certainly be impeached. The current House speaker only avoided a vote to do so before the midterms by adjourning early. And Pentagon insiders, who despair of Hegseth, still have some sway with Republican senators. But, given Trump would presumably be opposed, it is still very unlikely.

Passing legislation to undermine the president is impossible because he can veto it, and a two-thirds majority in both chambers is required to override his veto. Democrats would no doubt quickly pass a vote to stop the Iran war, assuming it is still going on when the new Congress meets in January, but Trump would veto. This can be useful for forcing the president and his allies to affirm their support for unpopular action, but it can’t force a change in policy.

The main exception is government funding, where the president will eventually agree to a compromise or parts of the government would be permanently shut down. The budget for the fiscal year that started last week has not been passed and the government is currently operating thanks to a “continuing resolution” that expires in December. We can expect much brinksmanship around this, probably ending with another continuing resolution and no budget. This will likely keep happening under the new Congress. Democrats will be under huge pressure not to agree to a budget and Trump won’t be willing to make the compromises necessary to force their hand. Equally, they will agree to continuing resolutions because they are unlikely to want to shut down the government for too long.

This may cause issues for the military in Iran. Separate from the budget, the White House has asked Congress for almost $70 billion in additional appropriations for the war, which has not yet been agreed. If Congress does not sign this off, it won’t force the US to stop fighting immediately — the administration can transfer money from other budgets — but it will create more pressure to end the war by constraining Pentagon finances over time.

Another option for escalation, assuming the administration is non-cooperative with investigations, would be to revive a dormant procedure called “inherent contempt.” This allows either chamber to arrest someone, run a trial, and impose a penalty itself. It has not been used since 1934 and is problematic for many reasons. Congress has very limited means of enforcing an arrest, and any attempt to do so would be immediately referred to the courts on habeas corpus grounds.

It has occasionally been mooted as a way to encourage compliance, most notably during the Watergate hearings. But in recent years it has been more seriously contemplated as norms around cooperation and bipartisanship have largely broken down. The Democrats discussed it publicly in 2019, when the Justice Department was blocking their investigations. And then in 2024, the House voted on a Republican proposal for inherent contempt against Biden’s attorney-general Merrick Garland for refusing to hand over audio clips of the president. It failed by just six votes, but would have seen Garland fined $10,000 a day until he handed over the recordings.

Democrats will be under a lot of pressure to try a similar approach, and they will probably have the necessary majority to win a House vote. They would likely use a similar mechanism — fines rather than imprisonment — to try to force compliance. Whether it worked would come down to the Supreme Court, which is still providing a lot of cover for Trump. But the court doesn’t side with him every time, and the judges will be thinking about their own future too. Senior Democrats have talked about increasing the number of Supreme Court justices if they win the presidency (which is possible, though it would require a filibuster-proof sixty-seat majority in the Senate or the abolition of the filibuster). Conservative justices will want to avoid giving too much ammunition to those who want to force this through.

The net effect of all this would not be to stop the Trump administration from doing damage. It could continue ICE enforcement, Justice Department intimidation and all the rest. A Democratic Congress would not be able to stop military action immediately or pass legislation to change policies.

But it would be highly incentivised to cause as much trouble as possible. Numerous investigations would tie up Trump’s aides and possibly leave them at personal risk of substantial fines. There are already nowhere near enough people in senior roles to manage the responsibilities of the US government, and quite a few more are leaving, so we would see a further reduction in administrative capacity. The Democrats would also seek to cause maximum embarrassment to elected Republicans by forcing them to go on the record in support of Trump’s most unpopular policies and to defend the man himself.

As long as Trump is alive, and assuming he does not voluntarily quit through boredom, this is a huge problem for the Republicans. Typically, a party will try to distance itself from an unpopular lame duck president and re-orient around a new nominee. But now they cannot because of Trump’s residual popularity with the MAGA crowd. J.D. Vance remains a strong favourite to be their next nominee, but he is tied to the Trump presidency and needs his endorsement. If the Republicans lose badly this time, they are not just at risk of losing the presidency but of the Democrats winning sixty Senate seats in 2028 and having a filibuster-proof majority to pass legislation and change the composition of the Supreme Court.

This will all have a significant effect on global politics. Trump will still try to throw his weight around internationally, but it will have less purchase when he is on the way out. Former allies, who are currently seeking alternative alliances, will feel there is a good chance of resurrecting some kind of relationship with the US under a Democratic administration and will therefore seek to maintain ties. But they will be less worried about speaking out about the problems caused by Trump. We have already seen something of a shift here, with right-wing leaders such as Giorgia Meloni becoming more strident in their criticism of him.

Meloni’s and Marine Le Pen’s distancing from Trump is particularly interesting because it is fracturing the global radical right alliance (something I thought might happen when I wrote about it last year). The UK right depends more heavily on the United States for media subscriptions, speaking gigs and policy ideas than the right in other European countries does. While falling support for Trump does not translate directly into a lower Reform vote share, it will magnify discomfort around points of comparison. Reform’s immigration policy is, for instance, dependent on ICE-style raids, and its spending cuts are inspired by DOGE. But if it moves to distance itself from Trump it could be attacked by right-wing commentators who rely on the US for their income.
Two years ago Trump’s second win dramatically shifted the mood of both American and global politics. His final decline would lead to another recalibration. •
